It also identifies negative feedback and the approximate −RF transimpedance, satisfying the full-credit rule.

answer.text:
The circuit is a current to voltage converter,
a transimpedance amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate AC ground, source driven by $I_{in}$,
drain loaded by $R_{D1}$. Common-gate stage.
* $M_{2}$ : source grounded, gate driven by the drain
of $M_{1}$, drain loaded by $R_{D2}$. Common-source stage.
* $R_{F}$ from drain of $M_{2}$ to source of $M_{1}$.

$R_{F}$ senses the output voltage in parallel,
shunt sampling, and returns a current in parallel
to the input, shunt mixing. It is voltage-current,
shunt-shunt feedback.

Put $V_{in}$ = AC voltage at source of $M_{1}$,
$V_{X}$ = AC voltage at drain of $M_{1}$ / gate of $M_{2}$,
$V_{out}$ = AC output voltage.

$g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1}$ for $M_{1}$, $g_{m2},r_{o2}$
for $M_{2}$, $M_{2}$ source grounded has no body effect.
Put $g_{m1}'=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$, $g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}$,
$g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$.

Polarity: $I_{in}\uparrow \to V_{in}\uparrow$.
CG is non-inverting: $V_{X}\uparrow$.
CS is inverting: $V_{out}\downarrow$.
Feedback current from input to output
$(V_{in}-V_{out})/R_{F}\uparrow$, i.e. it
steals more of $I_{in}$ from the forward path.
Negative feedback.

Two-port $Y$ of $R_{F}$:

$$Y_{11}=Y_{22}=1/R_{F},\quad Y_{12}=Y_{21}=-1/R_{F}$$

For shunt sampling, input loading is with
$V_{out}=0$. For shunt mixing, output loading
is with $V_{in}=0$.

Loaded open loop: forward CG+CS with $R_{F}$
to ground at input, $R_{F}$ to ground at
output. Feedback factor

$$I_{f}=Y_{21}V_{out},\quad \beta=-\frac{1}{R_{F}} $$

in the sense $V_{out}=A_{OL}(I_{in}+V_{out}/R_{F})$,
i.e.

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1-A_{OL}/R_{F}} $$

$A_{OL}<0$ is the loaded transimpedance.
Loop gain

$$T=-\frac{A_{OL}}{R_{F}}>0$$

and

$$Z_{T}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1+T}=-R_{F}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

Ideal $T\gg 1$: $Z_{T}\approx -R_{F}$.

Loaded forward gain. Looking into source of
CG with $R_{D1}$ at drain:

$$R_{in1}= \frac{r_{o1}+R_{D1}}{1+g_{m1}'r_{o1}}$$

$$\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}'}\;\;r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$$

With $V_{in}$ given,

$$V_{X}/V_{in}=A_{v1}=(g_{m1}'+g_{ds1})(r_{o1}\parallel R_{D1})$$

KCL at $X$: $V_{X}/R_{D1}+i_{d1}=0$,
$i_{d1}=-g_{m1}'V_{in}+g_{ds1}(V_{X}-V_{in})$.

CS stage loaded by $R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$:

$$V_{out}/V_{X}=A_{v2}=-g_{m2}(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

Input voltage from $I_{in}$:

$$V_{in}/I_{in}=R_{F}\parallel R_{in1}=R_{in,open}$$

Hence

$$A_{OL}=R_{in,open}\,A_{v1}\,A_{v2}$$

$$A_{OL}=-(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{v1}g_{m2}
(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

$$T=\frac{(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{v1}g_{m2}
(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})}{R_{F}}$$

Neglecting $r_{o}$, $g_{mb}$:

$$R_{in1}\approx 1/g_{m1},\;A_{v1}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}$$

$$A_{OL}\approx -\frac{R_{F}}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}
g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

$$T\approx \frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})}
{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}$$

$$Z_{T}\approx -R_{F}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

i.e.

$$Z_{T}\approx \frac{-g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})
\frac{R_{F}}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}}{1+T}$$

Closed loop input impedance is $V_{in}/I_{in}$
with feedback. Feedback theory for shunt mixing:

$$R_{in,closed}=\frac{R_{in,open}}{1+T}$$

$$R_{in,closed}=\frac{R_{F}\parallel R_{in1}}{1+T}$$

$\approx (R_{F}\parallel 1/g_{m1})/(1+T)$.
For large $T$ this is $\approx 0$, virtual ground.
Direct KCL gives $R_{in}=R_{F}/(1+g_{m1}'R_{F}+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{2})$
with $R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$.

Closed loop output impedance: set $I_{in}=0$,
drive output with $V_{t}$, measure $I_{t}$.

With $I_{in}=0$:

$$\frac{V_{t}-V_{in}}{R_{F}}=\frac{V_{in}}{R_{in1}}$$

$$V_{in}=V_{t}\frac{R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}$$

$$V_{X}=A_{v1}V_{in}$$

$$I_{t}=V_{t}/R_{D2}+g_{m2}V_{X}+g_{ds2}V_{t}
+(V_{t}-V_{in})/R_{F}$$

$$\frac{1}{R_{out}}=\frac{1}{R_{D2}}+g_{ds2}
+\frac{1+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{out}= \left[\frac{1}{r_{o2}\parallel R_{D2}}
+\frac{1+g_{m2}A_{v1}R_{in1}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}\right]^{-1}$$

Neglecting $r_{o}$, $g_{mb}$:

$$\frac{1}{R_{out}}\approx \frac{1}{R_{D2}}
+\frac{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}$$

$$R_{out}\approx R_{D2}\parallel
\frac{R_{F}+1/g_{m1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}}$$

For $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$ and large $T$,
$R_{out}\approx R_{D2}/(1+T)$. Shunt
sampling lowers output impedance toward zero.

In summary, large forward gain makes it an
almost ideal transimpedance $-R_{F}$ with
small input impedance and small output
impedance. The loop has two high impedance
nodes $X$ and output, so stability and
bandwidth are set by poles at $R_{D1}$ and
$R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}$ with device and
load capacitances.

answer.text:
This is a transimpedance amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate grounded for ac, signal in the
source, signal out the drain $X$.
Common-gate with load $R_{D1}$.

* $M_{2}$ : source grounded, signal in the gate $X$,
signal out the drain $V_{out}$. Common-source with
load $R_{D2}$.

* $R_{F}$ from output to input.

Let small signal node voltages be $v_{in}$ at
the $I_{in}$ node, $v_{X}$, $v_{out}$.
Ignore body for the moment. Put

$$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}\;,\;r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$$
$$R_{D1}'=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\;,\;
  R_{D2}'=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$M_{1}$: $v_{gs1}=-v_{in}$,
$v_{ds1}=v_{X}-v_{in}$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

enters the drain, leaves the source.

$M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=v_{X}$,
$v_{ds2}=v_{out}$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{X}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

enters the drain.

### Feedback polarity and type

$R_{F}$ senses $v_{out}$, i.e. output voltage,
returns a current to the input node where it
sums with $I_{in}$. Shunt at output,
shunt at input : voltage-current,
shunt-shunt feedback.

Check sign: let $v_{out}\uparrow$.
Current $(v_{out}-v_{in})/R_{F}$ into
the input node $\uparrow$, $v_{in}\uparrow$.

$v_{in}\uparrow \to v_{gs1}\downarrow \to
i_{d1}\downarrow \to$ drop in $R_{D1}\downarrow
\to v_{X}\uparrow \to i_{d2}\uparrow \to
v_{out}\downarrow$.

The rise is opposed. Negative feedback.

For large loop gain the input is a virtual ground
and all of $I_{in}$ flows in $R_{F}$:

$$v_{out}\approx -I_{in}R_{F}$$

i.e. an inverting transimpedance $-R_{F}$.

### Small signal equations

KCL X, no gate current:

$$\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}+i_{d1}=0 \tag{2}$$

KCL input:

$$I_{in}+i_{d1}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0 \tag{1}$$

KCL output:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+
\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0 \tag{3}$$

From (2):

$$\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}(-v_{in})
+g_{ds1}(v_{X}-v_{in})=0$$

$$v_{X}=v_{in}\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}
{1/R_{D1}+g_{ds1}} =A_{1}v_{in}$$

$$A_{1}=(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})R_{D1}'\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}'$$

Positive CG gain.

Also $i_{d1}=-v_{X}/R_{D1}=-G_{1}v_{in}$ where

$$G_{1}=\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}
 =\frac{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}$$

$1/G_{1}$ is the input resistance into the
CG source with drain load:

$$R_{in1}=1/G_{1}= \frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}
{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}$$

Then (1) becomes

$$I_{in}=v_{in}\left(G_{1}+\frac1{R_{F}}\right)
-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{F}} \tag{1'}$$

(3) becomes

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_{D2}'}+\frac1{R_{F}}\right)
+v_{in}\left(g_{m2}A_{1}-\frac1{R_{F}}\right)=0
\tag{3'}$$

i.e. with loading the $v_{in}\to v_{out}$ gain is

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{1/R_{D2}'+1/R_{F}}$$

$\approx -g_{m2}A_{1}(R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$.
The $1/R_{F}$ is direct feedthrough.

Solving (1')(3'):

$$R_{T}=\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}
 =-\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{(G_{1}+1/R_{F})(1/R_{D2}'+1/R_{F})
 +(g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F})/R_{F}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{T}=\frac{1-g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$$=-R_{F}\frac{1-1/g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}}
{1+G_{1}/g_{m2}A_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})
/g_{m2}A_{1}R_{D2}'}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$,
$A_{1}=g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $G_{1}=g_{m1}$,
$R_{D2}'=R_{D2}$:

$$R_{T}\approx
\frac{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}}
{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}+g_{m1}+(1+g_{m1}R_{F})/R_{D2}}$$

If $g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}\gg1$ and denominator
dominated by $g_{m2}A_{1}$,

$$R_{T}\approx -R_{F}$$

Check $R_{F}\to\infty$ : open loop transimpedance

$$R_{T,open}=-g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}'$$

indeed $v_{in}=I_{in}/G_{1}$,
$v_{X}=A_{1}v_{in}=R_{D1}I_{in}$,
$v_{out}=-g_{m2}R_{D2}'v_{X}$.

In two-port terms, voltage sampling, current
mixing loads the A-circuit with $R_{F}$ to
ground at input for $v_{out}=0$ and $R_{F}$
to ground at output for $v_{in}=0$.
Open loop with loading:

$$A_{OL}=\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}\Big|_{load}
 =-A_{1}g_{m2}(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})
 (R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$$

Loop gain, neglecting feedthrough,

$$T=\frac{|A_{OL}|}{R_{F}}
 \approx g_{m2}A_{1}(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})
 \frac{R_{D2}'}{R_{D2}'+R_{F}}$$

More exactly

$$T=\frac{g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F}}
{(G_{1}+1/R_{F})(1+R_{F}/R_{D2}')}$$

so that $R_{T}=-R_{F}T/(1+T)$.

Input resistance $v_{in}/I_{in}$ from (1')(3'):

$$R_{in}=\frac{1+R_{F}/R_{D2}'}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$\to 1/G_{1}=R_{in1}$ for $R_{F}\to\infty$.
For large $T$,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}$$

where $|A_{v}|\approx g_{m2}A_{1}
(R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F})$. Feedback lowers
the already low CG $1/g_{m1}$ by $1+T$.

Output resistance: set $I_{in}=0$ open,
apply $v_{x}$ at output, measure $i_{x}$.
Then $-G_{1}v_{in}+(v_{x}-v_{in})/R_{F}=0$,
$v_{in}=v_{x}/(1+G_{1}R_{F})$,
$v_{X}=A_{1}v_{in}$,

$$i_{x}=v_{x}/R_{D2}'+g_{m2}v_{X}+G_{1}v_{in}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}
 =\frac{1+G_{1}R_{F}}
{g_{m2}A_{1}+G_{1}+(1+G_{1}R_{F})/R_{D2}'}$$

$\to R_{D2}'$ for $R_{F}\to\infty$.
Feedback lowers it by $\approx 1+T$.

With body effect on $M_{1}$, whose body is
substrate ground, replace $g_{m1}$ by
$g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_{1}$ and $G_{1}$.

DC bias is through $R_{F}$: $I_{RD1}=I_{D1}$,
$I_{RF}=I_{D1}+I_{in,DC}$ flows input$\to$output,
$I_{D2}=I_{RD2}+I_{RF}$. $V_{X}=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}$,
$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{RD2}R_{D2}$, $V_{in}-V_{out}
=I_{RF}R_{F}$. $V_{b}$ sets $V_{gs1}$ and $I_{D1}$,
$V_{X}$ sets $I_{D2}$. Proper sizing must keep
both in saturation despite DC drop in $R_{F}$.

answer.text:
The circuit is a two stage shunt-shunt feedback
transimpedance amplifier.  $M_{1}$ is a common gate input
device, $M_{2}$ a common source gain device, $R_{F}$ returns
a current from the output to the input node.  $V_{b}$ is ac
ground.  Let the (small signal) voltage at the source of
$M_{1}$ be $v_{in}$, at $X$ be $v_{x}$, at the output $v_{out}$.
Body effect is absent for the symbols as drawn; for a common
substrate replace $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in what follows.

In dc, with $I_{in}$ the dc value of the input source,

$$\begin{aligned}
v_{in0}&=V_{b}-V_{GS1}, \qquad v_{x0}=V_{GS2}\\
I_{D1}&=\frac{V_{DD}-v_{x0}}{R_{D1}},\qquad 
I_{D2}= \frac{V_{DD}-v_{out0}}{R_{D2}}+\frac{v_{in0}-v_{out0}}{R_{F}}\\
\frac{v_{in0}-v_{out0}}{R_{F}}&=I_{in0}+I_{D1}
\end{aligned}$$
i.e. $R_{F}$ also carries bias current.  Saturation requires
$v_{x}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}$ for $M_{1}$ and $v_{out}\ge v_{x}-V_{TH2}$
for $M_{2}$.

### Small signal forward path

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{d1}&=-g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}-v_{in}}{r_{o1}}\\
i_{d2}&=\phantom{-}g_{m2}v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}
\end{aligned}$$

Node $X$: $v_{x}/R_{D1}+i_{d1}=0$, whence

$$
 \frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=A_{1}
      =\Bigl(g_{m1}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\Bigr)\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)
      \approx g_{m1}\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr) \tag{1}
$$
the usual non-inverting CG gain.  The resistance looking
into the source of $M_{1}$ alone, i.e. with $R_{F}$ removed, is

$$
R_{in,CG}=\frac{v_{in}}{-i_{d1}}=\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}
          =\frac{R_{D1}}{A_{1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}} . \tag{2}
$$

Node out, with $R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$,

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0
$$

$$
\,v_{out}= \bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
        \left(\frac{v_{in}}{R_{F}}-g_{m2}v_{x}\right)\,
$$

i.e. the (loaded) voltage gain from the input node is

$$
 A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)\Bigl(\frac1{R_{F}}-g_{m2}A_{1}\Bigr)
      \approx -g_{m2}A_{1}\bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
      \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})  \tag{3}
$$
for $g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}\gg1$ and $R_{F}\gg R_{2}$.  The $1/R_{F}$
term is the feedforward through $R_{F}$.  An increase in
$v_{in}$ raises $v_{x}$ and lowers $v_{out}$: the loop
through $R_{F}$ is negative.

### Closed loop transimpedance and input resistance

KCL at the input, with $i_{RF}$ taken from output to input
as drawn,

$$
I_{in}+i_{RF}=-i_{d1}=\frac{v_{in}}{R_{in,CG}},\qquad
i_{RF}=\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}
$$

so that

$$
 I_{in}= \frac{v_{in}}{R_{in,CG}}+\frac{v_{in}-v_{out}}{R_{F}}
       =v_{in}\!\left[\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1-A_{v}}{R_{F}}\right]. \tag{4}
$$

Hence

$$
\,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_{in}}{I_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,1/R_{in,CG}+ (1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      =R_{in,CG}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}}{1-A_{v}}\,  \tag{5}
$$

and the transimpedance is

$$
\;
{\cal R}_{T}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}=A_{v}R_{in}
      =\frac{A_{v}}{\,1/R_{in,CG}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      =\frac{-R_{F}}{\,1-\dfrac{1+R_{F}/R_{in,CG}}{A_{v}}\,}\;
\tag{6}
$$

With $|A_{v}|\gg 1+R_{F}/R_{in,CG}$, i.e. with effective loop
gain

$$
T_{eff}\approx\frac{|A_{v}|}{R_{F}/R_{in,CG}}
      \approx\frac{g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}{R_{F}}\gg1,
$$

$$\;{\cal R}_{T}\approx -R_{F},\qquad 
       R_{in}\approx\frac{R_{in,CG}}{1+T_{eff}}\approx
       \frac{1}{g_{m1}+ (1+|A_{v}|)/R_{F}}\;  $$

In this limit $v_{in}=I_{in}R_{in}$ is very small - a quasi
virtual ground - and from $I_{in}+i_{RF}=v_{in}/R_{in,CG}$

$$
i_{RF}\approx -I_{in},
$$

i.e. essentially all of $I_{in}$ flows (input to output) in
$R_{F}$, producing $v_{out}\approx-I_{in}R_{F}$; only the small
error current $v_{in}/R_{in,CG}$ enters $M_{1}$ and is amplified.
Increasing $R_{F}$ increases $|{\cal R}_{T}|$ but decreases
$T_{eff}$.

For $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$,
$A_{1}=g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $R_{in,CG}=1/g_{m1}$,
$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! R_{F})$.

### Output resistance

Put $I_{in}=0$ (input source open) and apply a test voltage
$v_{t}$ at the output.  Then $v_{in}=v_{t}R_{in,CG}/(R_{in,CG}+R_{F})$,
$v_{x}=A_{1}v_{in}$, and

$$
\;
R_{out}= \frac{1}{\,1/R_{2}+ \dfrac{1+g_{m2}A_{1}R_{in,CG}}{R_{F}+R_{in,CG}}\,}
       =R_{2}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}+R_{in,CG}}{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}}
       \approx (R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}}{g_{m2}R_{D1}}\;
\tag{7}
$$
since $A_{1}R_{in,CG}=R_{D1}$.  Feedback lowers $R_{out}$ below
$R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$; with an external load replace
$R_{D2}$ by $R_{D2}\parallel R_{L}$ throughout.

In short: $M_{1}$ gives a $\approx1/g_{m1}$ input termination and
first voltage gain $g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $M_{2}$ gives the second,
inverting, gain, and shunt-shunt feedback through $R_{F}$ sets
$v_{out}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}$, and further lowers both $R_{in}$
and $R_{out}$ by about the loop gain.  This is the standard
low-input-impedance TIA used e.g. at a photodiode input; the
poles at $X$ and at the output are inside the loop, so in
practice a small capacitor is usually placed across $R_{F}$
for stability.

answer.text:
The circuit is a two stage transimpedance amplifier
with shunt-shunt feedback.  $I_{in}$ is e.g. a photodiode
current.  Let $A$ be the input node, the source of $M_{1}$,
$v_{a}$ its small signal voltage, $v_{x}$ the voltage at $X$ and
$v_{o}$ the output voltage.  As drawn the bodies are tied to the
sources, so there is no body effect.  $V_{b}$ and $V_{DD}$ are ac
grounds.

$M_{1}$ is a common gate device, gate at the fixed bias $V_{b}$,
drain loaded by $R_{D1}$.  $M_{2}$ is a common source device,
gate at $X$, drain loaded by $R_{D2}$.  $R_{F}$ returns a current
proportional to $v_{o}$ to the input node $A$: output voltage
sampling, current mixing at the input, i.e. shunt-shunt
negative feedback.  An increase of $i_{in}$ raises $v_{a}$,
lowers $V_{GS1}$ and $I_{D1}$, raises $v_{x}$, raises $I_{D2}$ and
lowers $v_{o}$; the current returned through $R_{F}$ opposes
$i_{in}$.  $A$ is a low impedance, approximately virtual earth,
node.

In dc, with $M_{1,2}$ in saturation,
$$\begin{aligned}
V_{A}&=V_{b}-V_{GS1}, &
V_{X}&=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}=V_{GS2},\\
V_{out}&=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D2},
\end{aligned}\qquad 
\begin{array}{ll}
V_{X}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}& M_{1}{\rm \ sat.}\\
V_{out}\ge V_{X}-V_{TH2}& M_{2}{\rm \ sat.}
\end{array}
$$
$R_{D1}$ thus sets $V_{GS2}$ and hence $I_{D2}$ for a given
$I_{D1}$.  The usable $|i_{in}|$ is about the available output
swing divided by $R_{F}$.

### Small signal gain

Put $R_{1}'=R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}$, $R_{2}'=R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$
($R_{2}'$ may include a load).  At $X$, $i_{d1}=-v_{x}/R_{D1}$ and

$$ 
\frac{v_{x}}{v_{a}}=
\frac{g_{m1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}{R_{D1}^{-1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}
\equiv A_{1}\approx g_{m1}R_{1}' >0
\tag{1}
$$
the usual CG voltage gain.  At the output, with
$i_{RF}=(v_{o}-v_{a})/R_{F}$ in the direction shown,

$$
\frac{v_{o}}{R_{D2}}+g_{m2}v_{x}+\frac{v_{o}}{r_{o2}}
      +\frac{v_{o}-v_{a}}{R_{F}}=0
$$
i.e.
$$
A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{o}}{v_{a}}
      =-\,\bigl(g_{m2}A_{1}-R_{F}^{-1}\bigr)\,
        \bigl(R_{2}'\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
      \approx -g_{m2}R_{2}'A_{1}
      \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}'R_{2}'<0 .
\tag{2}
$$
The CG stage gives the low input impedance and isolates the
large input capacitance from the Miller effect of $M_{2}$;
$M_{2}$ supplies most of the loop gain.

KCL at $A$, the current into the source of $M_{1}$ being
$v_{x}/R_{D1}$,

$$
 i_{in}= \frac{v_{x}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{v_{a}-v_{o}}{R_{F}}
       =v_{a}\!\left[G_{in1}+\frac{1-A_{v}}{R_{F}}\right],
\qquad 
G_{in1}\equiv\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}
      =\frac{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}{R_{D1}+r_{o1}} .
\tag{3}
$$
$1/G_{in1}=(R_{D1}+r_{o1})/(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})\approx1/g_{m1}$ is the
resistance looking into the source of $M_{1}$ with $R_{F}$ removed.
Hence the closed loop transimpedance is

$$
\,R_{m}\equiv\frac{v_{o}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{A_{v}}{\,G_{in1}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      \approx
      -\,\frac{R_{F}}
             {\,1+\dfrac{1+G_{in1}R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}\,}\,
\tag{4}
$$

with loop gain, in this notation,
$T\approx |A_{v}|/(1+G_{in1}R_{F})$.
For $T\gg1$, i.e. $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}'R_{2}'\gg 1+g_{m1}R_{F}$,

$$
\,v_{o}/i_{in}\;\approx\;-R_{F}\,
$$

to an accuracy $\sim 1/T$, essentially independent of
$g_{m},R_{D},r_{o}$.  In particular $i_{RF}=(v_{o}-v_{a})/R_{F}
\approx -i_{in}$: incrementally almost all of $i_{in}$ flows
in $R_{F}$, the source current of $M_{1}$ changing very little.
The minus sign is the reference direction of $i_{RF}$ in the
figure.

### Input and output resistance

From (3)

$$
\,R_{in,cl}=\frac{v_{a}}{i_{in}}
   =\frac{1}{G_{in1}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}}
   =\Bigl(\frac1{G_{in1}}\Bigr)\Big\|\frac{R_{F}}{1-A_{v}}
   \approx\frac{R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}\ll\frac1{g_{m1}}\,  .
\tag{5}
$$
Shunt feedback at the input lowers the already low CG input
resistance by $\sim 1+T$.

With $i_{in}$ open, a test voltage at the output gives, for
$r_{o}\to\infty$ for brevity,

$$
R_{out,cl}=
\left[\frac1{R_{D2}}+
\frac{g_{m1}\bigl(1+g_{m2}R_{D1}\bigr)}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}
\right]^{-1}
\approx
\bigl(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\bigr)\;\Big\|\;
\frac{R_{F}+1/g_{m1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{1}'}\;,
\tag{6}
$$
i.e. voltage sampling lowers the output resistance well below
$R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$.  Feedback also improves linearity
and desensitises $R_{m}$ to device parameters, at the cost of
gain set accurately, and essentially only, by $R_{F}$.

### Frequency response, trade offs

There are poles at $A$, at $X$ and at the output,
$$\omega_{a}\sim\frac1{R_{in}C_{in}},\qquad
  \omega_{x}\sim\frac1{R_{1}'C_{X}},\qquad
  \omega_{o}\sim\frac1{R_{2}'C_{o}},$$
$C_{in}$ being the photodiode plus $C_{gs1}$ capacitance,
$C_{X}$ containing $C_{gs2}$ and the Miller multiplied
$C_{gd2}$, $C_{o}$ the load capacitance.  Feedback moves the
input pole up by $\approx 1+T$, but $\omega_{x}$ and $\omega_{o}$
are inside the loop; if they approach the loop crossover the
response peaks and can become unstable.  In practice a small
$C_{F}$ is usually put across $R_{F}$ to compensate the
$C_{in}$-$R_{F}$ pole.

Increasing $R_{F}$ increases $|R_{m}|$ directly, but lowers
$T\propto R_{F}^{-1}$ for large $R_{F}$, lowers bandwidth,
and its thermal noise current $4kT/R_{F}$ is input referred
directly.  Larger $g_{m1}$ lowers $R_{in}$, input referred
noise and the error in (4), at the cost of power and $C_{in}$.
Larger $R_{D1}R_{D2}$ increase $|A_{v}|$ and $T$ but cost
headroom and lower $\omega_{x},\omega_{o}$.  This CG-CS
shunt-feedback form is the standard wideband optical receiver
front end: $R_{m}\approx-R_{F}$, very low $R_{in}$, low
$R_{out}$, bandwidth largely set by $R_{F}C_{in}$ and the
$X$ and output poles.  If $M_{1}$'s body is the common substrate,
replace $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_{1}$ and $G_{in1}$.

The circuit is a two stage, shunt-shunt feedback
transimpedance amplifier.  $I_{in}$ is injected into a low
impedance node, $R_{F}$ returns a current proportional to
$V_{out}$ to that node, and

$$R_{m}\equiv {V_{out}\over I_{in}}\approx -R_{F}\qquad 
{\rm for\; large\; loop\; gain}$$

$M_{1}$ is a common gate device, gate at a-c ground at $V_{b}$,
input at its source, output at its drain, node $X$.
$M_{2}$ is a common source device, gate at $X$, output at its
drain.  Hence from the input node, call its small signal
voltage $v_{i}$, to $X$ the gain is positive, from $X$ to
$V_{out}$ negative, and from $I_{in}$ to $V_{out}$ negative.
$R_{F}$ is voltage sampling at the output and current mixing
in shunt at the input: a voltage-shunt feedback amplifier
whose stabilized quantity is $V_{out}/I_{in}$.

### Bias

With $V_{I}$ the d-c voltage at the source of $M_{1}$,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{b}-V_{I}, & I_{D1}&=f(V_{GS1})\\
V_{X}&=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}\\
V_{GS2}&=V_{X}, & I_{D2}&=f(V_{X})\\
V_{out}&=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D2}\\
V_{I}-V_{out}&=(I_{D1}+I_{in,dc})R_{F}
\end{aligned}$$

the last being KCL at the input node; the d-c current of
$M_{1}$ returns through $R_{F}$ to the output.  Saturation
requires in particular
$V_{X}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}$ for $M_{1}$ and
$V_{out}\ge V_{X}-V_{TH2}$ for $M_{2}$.  The $R_{F}$ loop
stabilises this point: e.g. $V_{out}\uparrow\to$ more current
returned through $R_{F}$ to the input $\to I_{D1}\downarrow\to
V_{X}\uparrow\to I_{D2}\uparrow\to V_{out}\downarrow$.

### Small signal gain

Put $g_{m1e}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ if the bulk of $M_{1}$ is at
a-c ground, $g_{m1}$ if bulk is tied to its source.
$V_{b}$ and $V_{DD}$ are a-c ground.  At node $X$,
$i_{d1}=-v_{x}/R_{D1}$ and
$i_{d1}=-g_{m1e}v_{i}+(v_{x}-v_{i})/r_{o1}$, i.e.

$$ 
{v_{x}\over v_{i}}\equiv A_{X}=
{(g_{m1e}r_{o1}+1)R_{D1}\over R_{D1}+r_{o1}}
\;\approx\;g_{m1e}\,(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})>0
$$
the familiar CG gain.  The resistance looking into the
source of $M_{1}$, with no $R_{F}$, is
$$
R_{C}={R_{D1}\over A_{X}}=
{R_{D1}+r_{o1}\over g_{m1e}r_{o1}+1}\approx {1\over g_{m1e}} .
$$

At the output, with $i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_{i})/R_{F}$ in the
direction shown,
$$
{v_{out}\over v_{i}}\equiv A_{v}=
{-g_{m2}A_{X}+1/R_{F}\over 
1/R_{D2}+1/r_{o2}+1/R_{F}}
\;\approx\;-g_{m2}A_{X}\,
\bigl(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)<0 .
$$
The $1/R_{F}$ term is the small non-inverting feedthrough
through $R_{F}$.  Unloaded,
$|A_{v0}|\approx A_{1}A_{2}$ with
$A_{1}\approx g_{m1e}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})$,
$A_{2}\approx g_{m2}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})$.

KCL at the input,
$\,i_{in}=v_{x}/R_{D1}+(v_{i}-v_{out})/R_{F}$, gives
$$
{ i_{in}\over v_{i}}=
{A_{X}\over R_{D1}}+{1-A_{v}\over R_{F}},\qquad
R_{in}={v_{i}\over i_{in}}=
R_{C}\;\Big\|\;{R_{F}\over 1-A_{v}} 
$$
i.e. the CG resistance $R_{C}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$
Miller-shunted by the inverting gain to the output.
The (exact within this model) transresistance is
$R_{m}=A_{v}R_{in}$.

Define the effective loop gain for current return
$$
T\approx {|A_{v0}|R_{C}\over R_{F}}
      ={g_{m2}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})R_{D1}\over R_{F}} .
$$
Then, for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,
$$
\,R_{in}\approx {R_{C}\over 1+T}\approx
{{1/g_{m1e}}\over 1+T}\,,\qquad
\,R_{m}\approx -R_{F}\,{T\over 1+T}
      =-\Bigl[R_{F}\;\Big\|\;
        g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})\Bigr]\,  .
$$
For $T\gg1$, $R_{m}\to -R_{F}$, $R_{in}\to R_{F}/|A_{v0}|$,
$v_{i}$ is almost clamped, and essentially all of
$\Delta i_{in}$ flows (opposite to the arrow shown) through
$R_{F}$: $v_{out}\approx -i_{in}R_{F}$.  The sign is as
expected: $i_{in}\uparrow\to v_{i}\uparrow$ slightly $\to
I_{D1}\downarrow\to v_{X}\uparrow\to I_{D2}\uparrow\to
v_{out}\downarrow$, and $R_{F}$ returns this to the input,
closing a negative loop.  Feedback also improves linearity
by $\sim 1+T$.

At the output, with $I_{in}$ open,
$$
R_{out}=
\Bigl[{1\over R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}}+
{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}\over R_{F}+R_{C}}\Bigr]^{-1}
\;\approx\;R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{F}\ {\rm large},
$$
in series with any external load $R_{L}\parallel R_{D2}$.

### Dynamics and tradeoffs

There are high impedance poles at $X$,
$\omega_{pX}\!\approx\!1/[(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})C_{X}]$
with $C_{X}$ including $C_{gs2}$ and Miller $C_{gd2}$, and at
the output,
$\omega_{po}\!\approx\!1/[(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})C_{out}]$,
plus the input pole at the very low $R_{in}$ with the
(source/photodiode) capacitance at the source of $M_{1}$ -
the reason for using a CG rather than a CS input.  Two
gain poles inside the $R_{F}$ loop readily give peaking in
$R_{m}(s)$; in practice a small $C_{F}$ across $R_{F}$ is
used for compensation.  Increasing $R_{F}$ raises the
ideal $|R_{m}|$ but lowers $T$, $R_{in}$ falls less, bandwidth
and phase margin suffer, and $4kT/R_{F}$ falls.  Increasing
$R_{D1},R_{D2}$ or $g_{m2}$ raises $A_{v0}$ and $T$ at the
cost of headroom and of the $X$ and output poles; increasing
$g_{m1e}$ lowers $R_{C}$, the input pole resistance and the
input referred noise.  Noise referred to the input is
dominated by $R_{F}$ and by $M_{1}$; noise of $M_{2},R_{D1},
R_{D2}$ is referred back divided by the first stage gain
$A_{X}$.

Based on the provided schematic, here is an analysis of the circuit.

### 1. Circuit Identification
The circuit is a **Transimpedance Amplifier (TIA)**. Its primary function is to convert an input current signal ($I_{in}$) into a proportional output voltage signal ($V_{out}$). The presence of the feedback resistor $R_F$ connecting the output back to the input node is the defining characteristic of a transimpedance configuration.

### 2. Component Breakdown
*   **Input Source ($I_{in}$):** A current source connected to ground, providing the input signal to the circuit.
*   **Feedback Resistor ($R_F$):** Connects the output node ($V_{out}$) back to the input node (the source of transistor $M_1$). This sets the transimpedance gain.
*   **Transistor $M_1$:** Likely configured as a **Common-Gate (CG)** amplifier.
    *   **Source:** Connected to the input node (where $I_{in}$ enters).
    *   **Gate:** Connected to a bias voltage $V_b$ (indicated by the label $V_b$).
    *   **Drain:** Connected to node $X$.
*   **Transistor $M_2$:** Likely configured as a **Common-Source (CS)** amplifier.
    *   **Gate:** Connected to node $X$ (potentially via a coupling capacitor, indicated by the symbol between node $X$ and the gate).
    *   **Source:** Connected to ground.
    *   **Drain:** Connected to the output node $V_{out}$.
*   **Load Resistors ($R_{D1}, R_{D2}$):**
    *   $R_{D1}$ connects node $X$ to the supply voltage $V_{DD}$. It acts as the load for the first stage ($M_1$).
    *   $R_{D2}$ connects the output node to $V_{DD}$. It acts as the load for the second stage ($M_2$).
*   **Node $X$:** An intermediate node connecting the drain of $M_1$, resistor $R_{D1}$, and the input to the second stage.
*   **Bias ($V_b$):** A DC bias voltage used to set the operating point of transistor $M_1$.

### 3. Operational Analysis
1.  **Input Stage ($M_1$):** The input current $I_{in}$ flows into the source of $M_1$. Because of the negative feedback through $R_F$, the voltage at the source of $M_1$ is held relatively constant (virtual ground approximation). The current $I_{in}$ flows through the channel of $M_1$ to its drain.
2.  **Voltage Conversion at Node $X$:** The current flowing through $M_1$ creates a voltage drop across resistor $R_{D1}$. Since $R_{D1}$ is connected to $V_{DD}$, the voltage at node $X$ is $V_X = V_{DD} - I_{D1} R_{D1}$. As $I_{in}$ increases, $I_{D1}$ increases, causing $V_X$ to decrease.
3.  **Second Stage ($M_2$):** The voltage at node $X$ is coupled to the gate of $M_2$. As $V_X$ decreases, the gate-source voltage of $M_2$ decreases, reducing the drain current $I_{D2}$.
4.  **Output Stage:** The output voltage is determined by the drop across $R_{D2}$: $V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{D2} R_{D2}$. Since $I_{D2}$ decreases when $I_{in}$ increases, $V_{out}$ increases.
5.  **Feedback:** The output voltage $V_{out}$ drives current through $R_F$ back to the input node. This negative feedback stabilizes the input voltage and determines the overall gain.

### 4. Transfer Function
Assuming high open-loop gain from the transistor stages, the circuit maintains the input node at a virtual ground. The relationship between input current and output voltage is approximately:

$$V_{out} \approx - I_{in} \cdot R_F$$

The negative sign indicates that an increase in input current results in a specific phase relationship at the output depending on the exact inversion of the stages, but typically a TIA is described by the magnitude of the transimpedance gain $R_F$.

### 5. Additional Observations
*   **Coupling Capacitors:** There appear to be capacitor symbols in the signal path (between node $X$ and $M_2$'s gate, and near $V_b$). This suggests the circuit might be designed for AC signals or RF applications (hinted by the label $i_{RF}$), blocking DC while passing AC signals.
*   **Supply:** The circuit uses a single positive supply $V_{DD}$.

The schematic is nothing more than a shunt-feedback (trans-impedance) amplifier that has been implemented with only two n-MOS devices and two passive load resistors.  
• node S (the junction that receives the photocurrent Iin, RF and the source of M1) is the “summing node” of the TIA;  
• M1 and RD1 constitute the first gain stage;  
• M2 and RD2 constitute the second gain stage and furnish the output node;  
• RF closes the dc- and a-c-feedback loop that forces the input node to a (nearly) constant potential so that almost the whole sensed current is conveyed through RF and translated into a voltage at Vout.

1. DC operating point  

   – Vb fixes the quiescent gate-source voltage of M1 → the drain current ID1.  
   – RD1 determines the dc value of VX (drain of M1 / gate of M2) :  
          VX ≃ VDD – ID1·RD1.  
   – The current that flows in M2 is therefore ≃ ID1 (neglecting gate current).  
     Choosing RD2 so that Vout ≃ VDD/2 gives the largest signal swing:  
          RD2 ≃ (VDD/2) / ID2.  
   – Both transistors must obviously remain in saturation for the expected
     excursion of Iin.

2. Small-signal model (ro of the MOSFETs is ignored for clarity).  

   Symbols: gm1 , gm2 ­– trans-conductances; RD1 , RD2 , RF ­– resistors;  
             vs , vx , vout – small-signal voltages at nodes S, X and OUT.

   a. Current generated by M1  
         id1 = gm1·(vgs1)  with vgs1 = Vb (ac ground) – vs ⇒ id1 = –gm1·vs.
   b. Voltage at node X (drop across RD1)  
         vx = – RD1·id1 = gm1·RD1·vs (negative sign kept explicit).  
   c. Output voltage produced by M2  
         vout = – gm2·RD2·vx = – gm2·RD2·(–gm1·RD1·vs)  
               =  (+) gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2 · vs.                  (1)

   Open-loop gain (from node S to node OUT)  
         A ≡ vout / vs =  gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2.                 (2)

   d. KCL at the summing node S (ro → ∞)  
         Iin + (vs – vout)/RF  – gm1·vs = 0.               (3)

   Combine (1), (2) and (3) to obtain the closed-loop trans-impedance:

         ZT ≡ vout / Iin = – RF · (1 + A) / (1 + A + gm1·RF).  (4)

   If the loop-gain A ≫ 1 and gm1·RF ≪ A (the usual design target),

         ZT  ≈  – RF           (ideal TIA behaviour)          (5)
         Zin ≡ vs / Iin ≈ RF / (1 + A) ≈ RF /A  ≪ 1 Ω.        (6)

   Hence the input node is a low-impedance “virtual ground” and the sensed
   current is almost completely forced through RF, converting it into the
   output voltage –Iin·RF.

3. Stability and bandwidth  

   There are two high-impedance nodes (X and OUT) → a two-pole loop.  
   The small capacitor that is drawn between VX and the gate of M2 is a
   Miller-compensation (or “lead”) capacitor that moves the dominant pole to
   node X and gives a left-half-plane zero to cancel part of the phase shift
   of the second pole, insuring ≥60° phase margin.

   A rough bandwidth estimate:  fbw ≃ 1 / [2π (RD1·CX)] , with CX the total
   capacitance at node X (RD1 is chosen far larger than 1/gm1 so that this
   pole dominates).

4. Noise  

   – Thermal noise of RF (4kT/RF) and channel noise of M1 are the dominant
     contributors at the amplifier input.  
   – Noise coming from M2 and RD2 is divided by the loop-gain before it is
     referred to the input (20- to 30-dB relief for A ≳ 10-30).

5. Practical design hints  

   • Make gm1 high (large W/L or a small drain current) to minimise the input
     impedance and to raise the loop-gain.  
   • RD1 must be big enough to give a large gain gm1·RD1 but still leave VX
     high enough to keep M1 in saturation over the full Iin range.  
   • Choose RD2 from the desired output swing and ID2.  
   • Vb is placed roughly one VGS(th) + 0.2-0.3 V above the desired quiescent
     input-node voltage (often 0 V for a photodiode TIA).  
   • Verify that the two poles are well separated or add the shown
     compensating capacitor.

6. Summary of key formulas  

   Open-loop gain:                 A = gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2  
   Closed-loop trans-impedance:    Vout / Iin ≈ – RF (for A ≫1)  
   Input impedance:                Zin ≈ RF /A                (very small)  
   Loop-gain:                      LG ≈ A (since β = 1 through RF)  

The circuit therefore behaves exactly like an operational-amplifier-based
inverting TIA, but it is implemented with the minimum amount of active
devices (only two MOSFETs) and gains its accuracy from the large product
gm1·gm2·RD1·RD2 rather than from a high-performance op-amp.

answer.text:
1. What the circuit is  
• The two MOSFETs and the two resistors form a two–stage voltage-amplifier.  
• The feedback resistor RF returns a portion of the output voltage to the input node, so the whole network is a shunt-shunt (current-voltage) feedback system.  
• Because the input variable is a current and the output variable is a voltage, the quantity of interest is the transimpedance   ZT = Vout / Iin.  
Typical use: front-end of a photodiode receiver, or any other application that needs a low-impedance node converting current to voltage.

2. DC bias (large-signal)  
M1 is biased as a common-gate device: its gate is held at the fixed voltage Vb, so its source node (the input node) sits roughly at  
    VS ≈ Vb – VGS1(on).  
The drain current of M1 flows through RD1, creating a dc voltage VX.  
The coupling capacitor insures that the dc bias of M2 is (almost) independent of M1, while ac variations at X are delivered to the gate of M2.  
M2 is a conventional common-source stage; its quiescent current flows through RD2 and sets the dc value of Vout.

(A very large resistor, or the bias network of the following stage, is usually placed in parallel with the capacitor so that the gate of M2 has a dc return; it has been omitted in the sketch for clarity.)

3. Small-signal model  
Let  

 vs  = small-signal voltage at the input node (source of M1)  
 vx  = small-signal voltage at node X (drain of M1, gate of M2)  
 vout = small-signal output voltage  
 gm1 , gm2 = transconductances of M1 and M2.  
Body effect and ro are neglected for clarity, but they can be added easily.

(i) Current through M1  
id1 = gm1 (vg1 − vs) = −gm1 vs                             (1)

(ii) Voltage at node X  
vx = −id1 RD1 = gm1 RD1 vs                                (2)

(iii) Output of M2  
id2 = gm2 vx  
vout = −id2 RD2 = −gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2 vs             (3)

Hence the (open-loop) voltage gain from the input node to the output node is  

 Av = vout / vs = −gm1 gm2 RD1 RD2.               (4)

4. Open-loop transimpedance (feedback open)  
Without RF, the input node sees the small impedance 1/gm1, so  

 vs = (1/gm1) Iin.  

Combining with (3) gives  

 ZOL = vout / Iin = −gm2 RD1 RD2.                (5)

5. Feedback relations  
The feedback current is  

 iRF = (vs − vout)/RF    (direction: from the input node toward the output, as indicated in the drawing)  

and the feedback factor that relates the fed-back current to the output voltage is  

 β = 1/RF.  

Loop-gain magnitude  
 T = β ZOL = −(gm2 RD1 RD2)/RF.                (6)

6. Closed-loop transimpedance  
Using the usual expression ZT = ZOL /(1 + βZOL):

 ZT = −gm2 RD1 RD2 /[1 − (gm2 RD1 RD2)/RF].    (7)

If |gm2 RD1 RD2| ≫ RF → |T| ≫ 1, the denominator is dominated by the second term and

 ZT ≈ RF    (with the expected sign inversion).           (8)

That is, the transimpedance accuracy is set by the passive element RF, while the active devices only have to provide sufficient loop gain.

7. Input impedance  
Rin = vs / Iin = ZT / Av  
  = RF /(1 + |T|) ≈ 1/(gm1)·(1/|T|) ≪ 1 Ω for large loop gain.  
A low Rin is precisely what a current source (e.g. photodiode) needs.

8. Bandwidth  
Because the loop gain multiplies the input node admittance by (1 + |T|), the −3 dB bandwidth roughly extends to  

 f3dB ≈ (1 + |T|) /[2π (CIN + CS1) / gm1]  

where CIN is the sensor capacitance and CS1 the parasitic capacitance at the source of M1.  
The dominant high-frequency poles are at node X (RD1 ‖ 1/gm2 with the capacitances of that node) and at the output node (RD2 with CLOAD).

9. Noise (spectral densities)  
Equivalent input-referred current noise:  

 Si,in ≈ 4kT γ gm1              (M1, dominant)  
     + 4kT/RF                (feedback resistor)  
     + 4kT γ gm2 /|T|²       (M2, suppressed by loop gain)  

so a large |T| both sets the gain and keeps the contribution of the second stage small.

10. Qualitative summary  
• M1 + RD1 create a transconductance stage whose low input impedance captures the external current.  
• The voltage at node X is ac-coupled to M2, which supplies high voltage gain.  
• The large gain around the shunt-shunt loop forces the input node to a virtual ground; consequently the closed-loop transimpedance is almost exactly RF, the input impedance is very small, and the bandwidth is widened by the loop-gain factor.  
• Proper choice of RD1, RD2, VB and the coupling capacitor value defines the bias point, maximises loop gain, and guarantees stability (phase margin).  
• Dominant noise comes from M1 and RF; the contribution of the second stage is suppressed by feedback.

In short, the circuit is a two-stage, gain-boosted transimpedance amplifier that provides precise gain ≈ RF, very low input impedance, wide bandwidth and low noise—an architecture well suited to high-speed or low-light photodetector interfaces.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as the common-source stage, and RF as feedback from the output to the input. But its signed loop equation uses 1 + βZOL with ZOL < 0, yielding a 1 − |T| denominator and an inconsistent transimpedance limit—effectively modeling the feedback with the wrong sign. This contradicts the required negative-feedback mechanism and caps the score at 2.

The schematic is nothing more than a two-stage, shunt–shunt-feedback MOS transimpedance amplifier (TIA).

• M1 (common–gate) performs the first current-to-voltage conversion:  
 IX = –gm1 VS flows into node X, and RD1 converts it into VX.

• A coupling capacitor ties VX to the gate of M2 (common-source).  
 For dc that capacitor is an open circuit, so M2 has no influence on the
 quiescent voltages; for signal frequencies above the high-pass corner it
 is effectively a short, so the voltage gain of M2 (≈ –gm2 RD2) is inserted
 in the feedback loop.

• RF returns the amplified signal to the input node, closing a shunt-shunt
 negative-feedback loop.  That loop simultaneously
 1) fixes the low-frequency transimpedance at –RF, so the gain is set with a
 single, precisely trimmable resistor, and  
 2) forces the input node close to ac ground, greatly reducing the input
 impedance and therefore increasing bandwidth.

Below is a concise dc and small–signal analysis (ro’s omitted for clarity;
add them in parallel with the RD’s if a more exact result is desired).

1.  dc operating point (Cc = open):
  ID1 = (VDD–VX)/RD1,  ID2 = (VDD–VOUT)/RD2  
 (The dc value of VS is set by the sum of IIN and the current through RF.)

2.  Small-signal equations (Cc = short):

 • Node X (drain of M1)  
  –gm1 VS + VX/RD1 = 0  ⇒ VX = gm1 RD1 VS (1)

 • Node OUT  
  VOUT/RD2 + gm2 VX + (VOUT – VS)/RF = 0  (2)

 • Input node (source of M1)  
  IIN = gm1 VS + (VS – VOUT)/RF         (3)

3.  Solve (1)–(3) for VOUT/IIN:

 Let A ≡ (1/RD2 + 1/RF) and B ≡ (1/RF – gm1 gm2 RD1)

 Zt ≡ VOUT/IIN = B RF /
        [(gm1 RF/RD2 + gm1) + (1/RD2) + gm1 gm2 RD1]  (4)

 If the loop-gain factor
  T ≃ gm1 gm2 RD1 RF / (1 + RF/RD2) ≫ 1

 then (4) collapses to the textbook result for a shunt-feedback TIA

  Zt ≈ –RF    (5)

 while the input impedance becomes

  ZIN = VS/IIN ≈ 1 / [gm1 (1 + gm2 RD1 + RF/RD2)]  (6)

 so the bandwidth is extended roughly by the multiplier  
 (1 + gm2 RD1 + RF/RD2) compared with a passive-RF TIA.

4.  Design hints

 • Choose gm1 from noise and head-room requirements.  
 • RD1 fixes VX ≃-gm1 RD1 VS; pick it so M1 never leaves saturation.  
 • Make gm2 RD2 as large as possible (voltage gain), respecting head-room.  
 • RF sets the wanted low-frequency transimpedance.  
 • Place the Cc high-pass corner at least one decade below the signal band
   so the feedback is active over the whole band but dc bias is untouched.

5.  Qualitative summary

 a. At dc the circuit is simply a resistor-feedback TIA (gain = –RF).  
 b. Above the Cc corner M2 amplifies the error at node X and drives it back
    to the input through RF; the loop makes the input look like a virtual
    ground, pushing the input pole and therefore the bandwidth upward.  
 c. The loop also cancels a large part of M1’s and M2’s channel noise,
    lowering the overall equivalent-input-noise current.

Hence the two-transistor / one-resistor network realises a wide-band, low-noise, well-defined-gain transimpedance amplifier well suited, for example, to photodiode front ends or wideband resistive-feedback LNAs.

- Assumes M₁ and M₂ are in saturation.

- V_b must be chosen so that M₁ is biased properly.

---

- **Input**: Current I_in.
- **Output**: Voltage V_out.
- **Gain**: Approximately **R_F** (transimpedance gain).
- **Key Mechanism**: Negative feedback forces source of M₁ to track V_b, making I_in flow through R_F to produce V_out.

---

> This circuit is a **transimpedance amplifier** with **local negative feedback** via resistor R_F. The output voltage is approximately **V_out = V_b + I_in × R_F**, so the small-signal transimpedance gain is **R_F**.     *   **Type:** This confirms the **Shunt-Shunt** feedback configuration.

It uses a Common-Gate stage ($M_1$) for low input impedance and a Common-Source stage ($M_2$) for gain. ## 1. What the circuit is

It is a **two‑stage CMOS amplifier with local (parallel‑parallel / shunt‑shunt) feedback**, used as a **transimpedance amplifier (TIA)**: the input is a *current* $I_{in}$, the output is a *voltage* $V_{out}$.

* **Stage 1 – $M_1$ (common‑gate):** gate at the AC‑ground bias $V_b$, input at the source, output at the drain (node $X$). The CG stage provides a low input resistance, which is desirable for a current input.
* **Stage 2 – $M_2$ (common‑source):** gate at $X$, source grounded, output at the drain $V_{out}$. Provides the voltage gain and inverts the phase.
* **Feedback element $R_F$:** connects $V_{out}$ back to the *source* of $M_1$ (the input node). The feedback current is $i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_s)/R_F$ (arrow direction in the figure). Because the feedback *samples the output voltage* and *mixes as a current* at the input node, it is **shunt‑shunt feedback**, which (i) makes the closed‑loop gain a transimpedance, (ii) *lowers* the input resistance, and (iii) *lowers* the output resistance.
* $R_{D1}, R_{D2}$ are the active (resistive) loads; $V_{DD}$ and $V_b$ are AC grounds.

## 2. DC operating point (qualitative)

$I_{in}$ (DC) is the bias current of $M_1$, but part of it also flows through $R_F$, so $I_{in}=I_{D1}+I_{RF,DC}$. The DC loop through $R_F$ self‑stabilises the bias. $V_b$ is chosen so that $M_1$ is in saturation ($V_X>V_{OV1}$ and $V_X>V_b$), and $V_X$ then biases $M_2$ on; $M_2$ must satisfy $V_{out}>V_X$ for saturation. The exact Q‑point is the solution of these coupled equations; the small‑signal analysis below is about that point.

## 3. Small‑signal model and node equations

Let $v_s$ = voltage of the $M_1$ source node, $v_x$ = node $X$, $v_o$ = $V_{out}$. Neglect $r_o$ and body effect (including $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ only adds parallel resistances and does not change the conclusions). With $v_{gs1}=-v_s$ and $v_{gs2}=v_x$:

* $M_1$ drain current (into drain): $i_{d1}=-g_{m1}v_s$
* $M_2$ drain current (into drain): $i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_x$

KCL at the three nodes (currents leaving the node = 0):

* Node $X$: $\ \dfrac{v_x}{R_{D1}}+i_{d1}=0 \ \Rightarrow\ v_x=g_{m1}R_{D1}\,v_s$
* Node $s$: $\ -i_{in}-i_{d1}+\dfrac{v_s-v_o}{R_F}=0 \ \Rightarrow\ i_{in}=g_{m1}v_s+\dfrac{v_s-v_o}{R_F}$
* Node $o$: $\ \dfrac{v_o}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+\dfrac{v_o-v_s}{R_F}=0$

## 4. Transimpedance gain $G_m=v_o/i_{in}$

Solving the three equations gives the exact (r_o‑free) result

$$\boxed{\,G_m=\frac{v_o}{i_{in}}=\frac{R_{D2}\,\big(1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F\big)}{1+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}\,}$$

**High‑loop‑gain limit** ($g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}\gg 1$): the gain is set almost entirely by the feedback resistor,

$$\boxed{\,v_o \approx -\,R_F\, i_{in}\,}$$

i.e. the circuit behaves as an ideal TIA with transimpedance $R_F$, **independent of the transistor parameters** – the main advantage of the feedback (good matching, linearity, and stability of gain). The minus sign reflects the inverting action of the common‑source stage.

## 5. Input and output resistance

**Input resistance** $Z_{in}=v_s/i_{in}$:

$$Z_{in}=\frac{R_{D2}+R_F}{1+g_{m1}R_{D2}+g_{m1}R_F+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}\ \approx\ \frac{1}{g_{m1}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+T}$$

The open‑loop input resistance of a CG stage is $\approx 1/g_{m1}$; the shunt feedback divides it by $(1+T)$, so $Z_{in}\ll 1/g_{m1}$. This low $Z_{in}$ is what lets the stage absorb the input current with a small $v_s$ (a "virtual" low‑impedance node).

**Output resistance** $Z_{out}$ (set $i_{in}=0$, drive $v_o$):

$$Z_{out}=\left[\frac{1}{R_{D2}}+\frac{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})}{1+g_{m1}R_F}\right]^{-1}\ \approx\ \frac{R_{D2}}{1+\dfrac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_F}}$$

Without feedback $Z_{out}\approx R_{D2}$; the shunt‑shunt feedback reduces it by the factor $\approx 1+g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_F$, giving a low, well‑defined output resistance – again a desirable TIA property.

## 6. Summary / design notes

* **Function:** CG + CS amplifier with shunt‑shunt feedback through $R_F$ → a low‑$Z_{in}$, low‑$Z_{out}$ transimpedance amplifier.
* **Gain:** $G_m = v_o/i_{in}$ is given exactly above and equals $\approx -R_F$ for large loop gain, hence robust against process/temperature variations of $g_m$ and $r_o$.
* **Impedances:** $Z_{in}$ and $Z_{out}$ are both suppressed by the feedback loop, improving bandwidth and the ability to drive/load the node.
* **Trade‑offs:** $R_F$ sets the gain but also loads the output (and, through the high $R_{D2}$, limits the loop gain and hence the actual gain‑boost and bandwidth); the $R_F$–$C_{out}$ pole and the CG node capacitance must be checked for stability (feedback can introduce a peaking/phase‑margin issue if $R_F$ is too large relative to the output impedance). Choosing $R_F$, $R_{D1}$, $R_{D2}$ and the biases so that $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_F\gg 1$ with adequate phase margin gives a TIA whose gain is essentially $R_F$.

## Circuit function

The schematic is a **two‑stage MOS amplifier with shunt–shunt (voltage‑sampling, current‑mixing) negative feedback** implemented by $R_F$. The input is a current $I_{in}$ and the output is a voltage $V_{out}$, so it is a **transresistance (transimpedance) amplifier**.

* $M_1$ (gate biased by the DC voltage $V_b$) works as a **common‑gate** front end: its source (call it node $S$) is the input node, its drain is node $X$.
* $M_2$ (gate = $X$, source = ground) works as a **common‑source** inverting gain stage; its drain is $V_{out}$.
* $R_{D1}, R_{D2}$ are the drain loads (and set the DC bias); $R_F$ feeds a portion of $V_{out}$ back as a current into node $S$.

Assume both devices are NMOS biased in saturation ($V_b$ chosen so that $M_1$ conducts; $X$ high enough to keep $M_2$ on).

## Small‑signal model (r_o ignored)

Let $v_x, v_s, v_{out}$ be the small‑signal voltages at $X$, $S$ and $V_{out}$; $V_b$ is an a.c. ground. The transistor currents are

$$i_{d1} = g_{m1}(0-v_s) = -g_{m1}v_s ,\qquad i_{d2} = g_{m2}v_x$$

Node equations:

* **Node X:** $\dfrac{v_x}{R_{D1}} - g_{m1}v_s = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; v_x = g_{m1}R_{D1}\,v_s$
* **Node S:** $i_{in} - g_{m1}v_s + \dfrac{v_{out}-v_s}{R_F} = 0$
* **Node $V_{out}$:** $\dfrac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}} + g_{m2}v_x + \dfrac{v_{out}-v_s}{R_F} = 0$

Solving for $v_{out}/i_{in}$ gives the exact mid‑band transresistance

$$\boxed{\,R_t = \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = \frac{R_{D2}\big(1 - g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F\big)}{1 + g_{m1}(R_{D2}+R_F) + R_{D2}\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}\,}$$

The feedback is **negative only when $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F > 1$** (otherwise $R_t>0$, i.e. positive feedback / unstable). In that region, and for large loop gain, the terms containing $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F$ dominate and

$$\boxed{\,R_t \approx -R_F\,}$$

i.e. the gain is set almost entirely by the feedback resistor and is independent of $g_m$, $R_{D1}$, $R_{D2}$. The minus sign means $V_{out}$ is inverted with respect to the injected current.

## Feedback interpretation

* Open‑loop forward path: $M_1$ (C‑G) gives $v_x = g_{m1}R_{D1}\,v_s$, $M_2$ (C‑S) gives $v_{out} = -g_{m2}R_{D2}\,v_x$; the input node presents $1/g_{m1}$ and the output node $R_{D2}$.
* Feedback factor (shunt–shunt): $H \approx 1/R_F$.
* Return ratio (loop gain):

$$T = \frac{R_{D2}}{R_{D2}+R_F}\,g_{m2}R_{D1} + \frac{1}{g_{m1}(R_{D2}+R_F)} \;\approx\; g_{m2}R_{D1}\quad (R_F \ll R_{D2})$$

Hence, with $T\gg 1$:

* **Closed‑loop transresistance** $R_t \approx R_t^{\,ol}/(1+T) \approx 1/H = -R_F$
* **Input resistance** (seen by $I_{in}$, node $S$) is reduced:

$$R_{in} = \frac{1}{g_{m1} + \frac{1}{R_{D2}+R_F} + \frac{R_{D2}}{R_{D2}+R_F}g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}} \;\approx\; \frac{1/g_{m1}}{1+T}\quad(\text{low})$$

* **Output resistance** is reduced:

$$R_{out} = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{R_{D2}} + \dfrac{g_{m1}(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})}{1+g_{m1}R_F}} \;\approx\; \frac{R_{D2}}{1+T}\quad(\text{low})$$

These are exactly the properties desired of a transimpedance amplifier: it accepts a current input (low $R_{in}$) and delivers a voltage output (low $R_{out}$), with a gain $|R_t|\simeq R_F$ that is insensitive to device‑parameter spread.

## DC bias (qualitative)

$V_b$ sets the $M_1$ bias current; $R_{D1}$ then fixes the DC level at $X$, which biases $M_2$. $R_{D2}$ and the $M_2$ current fix the DC level of $V_{out}$, and $R_F$ carries the DC bias current $I_{RF} = (V_S - V_{out})/R_F$. The designer chooses $V_b$ and the loads so that both transistors sit in saturation and the loop‑gain condition $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_F \gg 1$ holds.

## Frequency / stability comment

The dominant pole is usually at node $X$, where the resistance is $\approx R_{D1}$ (since $M_2$'s gate draws no current and $M_1$'s drain is high‑impedance); the output pole is at higher frequency because $R_{out}$ is low. The mid‑band gain $-R_F$ is desensitised by $1+T$, but $T$ rolls off at the $X$ pole, so the closed‑loop bandwidth and phase margin must be checked (the $R_F$ network and the parasitic capacitances at $X$ and $V_{out}$ determine the frequency at which $T$ falls to unity).

**Summary:** the circuit is a shunt–shunt negative‑feedback transimpedance amplifier. Its small‑signal transresistance is given exactly by the boxed expression above and, in the normal high‑loop‑gain design, reduces to $v_{out}/i_{in} \approx -R_F$, with low input and low output resistance.

## 1. What the circuit is

It is a **two‑stage transresistance (current‑in / voltage‑out) amplifier** with **shunt–shunt (parallel–parallel) negative feedback** through $R_F$.

| Block | Device | Configuration | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1st stage | $M_1$ (gate = $V_b$) | **Common‑gate** | current buffer: forces $i_{d1}\approx i_{in}$, presents a *low* impedance at node $S$ |
| 2nd stage | $M_2$ (source = gnd) | **Common‑source** | voltage gain + **inversion**, output taken at the drain |
| $R_{D1},R_{D2}$ | | loads / DC paths | set the DC currents and the bias point of $M_2$ |
| $R_F$ | | feedback | samples $V_{out}$ (shunt) and returns a **current** to node $S$ (shunt mixing with $i_{in}$) |

The input current $i_{in}$ is injected *in parallel* at node $S$ (the source of $M_1$), and the feedback current $i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_s)/R_F$ is also injected *in parallel* at the same node → **shunt mixing**. At the output, $R_F$ is in *parallel* with the output node → **shunt sampling**. Hence the closed‑loop quantity that is stabilised is the **transresistance** $R_{out}=v_{out}/i_{in}$.

### Polarity (negative feedback)
$ i_{in}\uparrow \Rightarrow v_s\uparrow \Rightarrow v_x\uparrow $ (CG, non‑inverting) $\Rightarrow v_{out}\downarrow $ (CS, inverting) $\Rightarrow i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_s)/R_F$ becomes negative, i.e. it *subtracts* from $i_{in}$ at node $S$. ✔ negative feedback.

## 2. DC operating point (qualitative)

A valid Q‑point exists with both MOSFETs in saturation. $V_b$ is chosen so that $M_1$ conducts; the DC current of $M_1$ flows through $R_{D1}$ (the gate of $M_2$ takes no current), fixing $V_X=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}$, which biases $M_2$. $M_2$ then pulls current through $R_{D2}$ and $R_F$. The DC value of $i_{RF}$ is $(V_{out}-V_S)/R_F$. The design must keep $V_X>V_{GS2}-V_{th2}$ and $V_X>V_{GS1}-V_{th1}$ (for saturation of $M_2$ and $M_1$ respectively). The small‑signal analysis below is valid around this point.

## 3. Small‑signal model and node equations

Let $v_x$, $v_s$, $v_{out}$ be the small‑signal voltages at nodes $X$, $S$ and $V_{out}$; $V_b$ is AC ground. Using $i_d=g_m v_{gs}+v_{ds}/r_o$ for each device:

* **Node X** (only $R_{D1}$ to AC‑gnd and the drain of $M_1$):
$$\frac{v_x}{R_{D1}}+g_{m1}(0-v_s)+\frac{v_x-v_s}{r_{o1}}=0 \tag{1}$$
* **Node S** ($i_{in}$ in, $R_F$ from $v_{out}$, source of $M_1$):
$$i_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_s}{R_F}+g_{m1}(0-v_s)+\frac{v_x-v_s}{r_{o1}}=0 \tag{2}$$
* **Node $V_{out}$** ($R_{D2}$, drain of $M_2$, $R_F$):
$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+g_{m2}(v_x-0)+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_{out}-v_s}{R_F}=0 \tag{3}$$

## 4. Transresistance gain

Solving (1)–(3) for $v_{out}/i_{in}$ and taking $r_{o1},r_{o2}\gg R$ gives the standard shunt–shunt form

$$\boxed{\;G=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=\frac{-R_F}{1+1/\mathcal{T}}\;}$$

with loop gain
$$\mathcal{T}\approx \frac{g_{m2}\,R_{D1}\,(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})}{R_F}\gg 1$$
(and a second, independent error term $\approx 1/(g_{m1}R_F)$ coming from $v_s\neq 0$).

**Asymptotic (ideal) value.** Because $\mathcal{T}\gg1$,

$$\boxed{\;\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}\;\approx\;-R_F\;}$$

*Physical picture:* negative feedback drives node $S$ to a **virtual ground** ($v_s\approx0$). With $v_s=0$, $M_1$ (a current buffer) draws essentially no extra current, so the whole $i_{in}$ is forced through $R_F$:
$$i_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-0}{R_F}=0\;\Rightarrow\;v_{out}=-i_{in}R_F .$$
The gain is therefore set almost entirely by the *passive* feedback element $R_F$ (hence very accurate and stable), while the active stages only provide the loop gain $\mathcal{T}$ and the inversion.

## 5. Input and output resistance

Shunt–shunt feedback reduces **both** resistances by $\approx(1+\mathcal{T})$:

* **Input resistance** (looking into $S$): open‑loop $\approx (r_{o1}+R_{D1})/(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})\approx 1/g_{m1}$; closed‑loop
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1/g_{m1}}{1+\mathcal{T}}\;\ll\;\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\quad(\text{ideal } \to 0)$$
  → excellent for accepting a *current* input.
* **Output resistance** (looking into $V_{out}$): open‑loop $\approx R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$; closed‑loop
$$R_{out}\approx \frac{R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}}{1+\mathcal{T}}\;\ll\;R_{D2}\quad(\text{ideal } \to 0)$$
  → excellent for delivering a *voltage* output.

## 6. Summary

The circuit is a **current‑to‑voltage converter** (transresistance amplifier). $M_1$ (CG) buffers the input current, $M_2$ (CS) supplies gain and inversion, and $R_F$ imposes shunt–shunt negative feedback that (i) fixes the closed‑loop transresistance at **$-R_F$**, (ii) collapses the input resistance toward zero (good for current drive), and (iii) collapses the output resistance toward zero (good for voltage drive). The accuracy of $v_{out}/i_{in}=-R_F$ improves as $g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})/R_F$ and $g_{m1}R_F$ increase.

## 1. Recognizing the structure

**Core amplifier (two stages):**
- **M₁** has its gate at the fixed bias $V_b$ (AC ground) and receives the signal at its **source** → **common‑gate (CG)** stage. Its load is $R_{D1}$ (node X).
- **M₂** has its source grounded and its gate at node X → **common‑source (CS)** stage. Its load is $R_{D2}$ (output node).
- Stage gains: CG is non‑inverting ($V_X/V_S = +g_{m1}R_{D1}$), CS is inverting ($V_{out}/V_X = -g_{m2}R_{D2}$). Overall the core is **inverting** from the input node to the output node.

**Feedback network:** $R_F$ connects the output node directly back to the input node.
- At the **output** it taps the output *voltage* (shunt/parallel sampling).
- At the **input** it returns a *current* $i_{RF}$ that sums with $I_{in}$ at the input node (shunt/parallel mixing).

⇒ **Shunt–shunt (parallel–parallel) feedback**, i.e. a **transimpedance amplifier** (current‑in, voltage‑out), the classic photodiode/front‑end TIA topology.

**Polarity check:** $I_{in}\uparrow \Rightarrow V_S\uparrow \Rightarrow V_X\uparrow \Rightarrow V_{out}\downarrow \Rightarrow$ more current is pulled *out* of the input node through $R_F$, opposing the rise of $V_S$ → **negative feedback**. ✔

## 2. Exact small‑signal solution (neglect $r_o$, body effect)

Node equations ($V_S$ = input node, $V_X$, $V_{out}$):

- Input node: $I_{in} = g_{m1}V_S + (V_S - V_{out})/R_F$
- Node X: $V_X = g_{m1}R_{D1}V_S$
- Output node: $V_{out}/R_{D2} + (V_{out}-V_S)/R_F + g_{m2}V_X = 0$

Solving, with $A = g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}$ and $a = R_{D2}/R_F$:

$$\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{-R_F\,(A - a)}{1 + A + g_{m1}R_F(1+a)},\qquad
R_{in} = \frac{R_F + R_{D2}}{1 + A + g_{m1}R_F(1+a)}$$

$$R_{out} = \frac{R_{D2}(1+g_{m1}R_F)}{1+g_{m1}R_F + g_{m1}R_{D2}(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})}$$

## 3. Feedback‑theory interpretation (insight)

Using the shunt–shunt loading rules ($R_F$ placed in parallel at both ports):

- **Open‑loop input resistance:** $R_{i,open} = R_F \parallel \tfrac{1}{g_{m1}}$
- **Open‑loop output resistance:** $R_{o,open} = R_D \!_2 \parallel R_F$
- **Open‑loop transresistance:** $R_0 = -\left(R_F \parallel \tfrac{1}{g_{m1}}\right) g_{m1}R_{D1}\, g_{m2}\,(R_{D2}\parallel R_F)$
- **Feedback factor:** $\beta = i_{RF}/V_{out} = 1/R_F$ (units A/V)
- **Loop gain:** $T = \beta |R_0| = \dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\parallel R_F)}{1+g_{m1}R_F}$

Closed loop (desensitivity factor $1+T$):

$$R_T = \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{R_0}{1+T},\qquad R_{in,cl} = \frac{R_{i,open}}{1+T},\qquad R_{out,cl} = \frac{R_{o,open}}{1+T}$$

**Deep‑feedback limit ($T \gg 1$):**

$$\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} \approx -R_F,\qquad R_{in,cl} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}T}\ (\text{very small}),\qquad R_{out,cl} \approx \frac{R_{D2}\parallel R_F}{T}\ (\text{very small})$$

## 4. Design interpretation

- **Why shunt–shunt is correct here:** the source is a *current* (infinite source resistance), so current mixing at a low‑impedance input node is ideal; the output is a *voltage*, so low output impedance is ideal. Feedback delivers both.
- **Gain set by a passive:** $V_{out}/I_{in} \approx -R_F$, insensitive to $g_m$'s and $R_D$'s; bandwidth is extended by ≈ $(1+T)$ compared with the open‑loop poles at node X and the output node.
- **DC biasing:** $R_F$ also closes the DC loop: $I_{D1} \approx I_{in} + (V_{out}-V_S)/R_F$, $V_S \approx V_b - V_{TH1}$, $V_X = V_{DD} - I_{D1}R_{D1}$, $V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{D2}R_{D2}$; $V_b$ and $R_{D1}, R_{D2}$ must keep both devices in saturation ($V_X > V_S - V_{TH}$… i.e. $V_{DS1}, V_{DS2} \ge V_{OV}$). Feedback stabilizes this operating point.
- **Refinements:** including $r_{o1}, r_{o2}$ replaces $R_{D1} \to R_{D1}\parallel R_{out,CG1}$ and $R_{D2} \to R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$, slightly reducing $T$; the exact expressions in §2 already include the (usually negligible) feed‑forward term through $R_F$ (the "$a$" terms).

**Bottom line:** this is a shunt–shunt‑feedback transimpedance amplifier (CG + CS core); its closed‑loop gain is $V_{out}/I_{in} \approx -R_F$ with input and output resistances lowered by the loop gain $1+T$, exactly what a current‑input/voltage‑output interface requires.

## 1. Recognizing the structure

- **M₁** (gate held at the fixed bias $V_b$) is a **common‑gate** stage: the input current $I_{in}$ is injected into its source node (call it node S, voltage $v_S$).
- **M₂** is a **common‑source** stage: its gate is driven by node X (drain of M₁, loaded by $R_{D1}$), and its drain drives $V_{out}$ through $R_{D2}$.
- **$R_F$** connects the output node back to the input node S. It is tied **in parallel (shunt) with the output node** → it *samples the output voltage*; it is tied **in parallel (shunt) with the input node** → it *returns a current* $i_{RF}$ that mixes with $I_{in}$.

⇒ **Shunt–shunt (parallel–parallel) feedback**, i.e. voltage‑sampling/current‑mixing ("voltage–current feedback" in Razavi's terminology). The circuit is a **transimpedance amplifier (current‑to‑voltage converter)**: ideally $V_{out}/I_{in} = $ const, with **low input and low output impedance**.

## 2. Polarity check (negative feedback)

$I_{in}\uparrow \Rightarrow v_S\uparrow \Rightarrow v_X = +g_{m1}R_{D1}v_S\uparrow$ (CG, non‑inverting) $\Rightarrow v_{out} = -g_{m2}(R_{D2}\|R_F)v_X\downarrow$ (CS, inverting). The falling $v_{out}$ pulls current from node S through $R_F$ toward the output, so the current entering M₁'s source, $g_{m1}v_S = I_{in}+i_{RF}$, is reduced → **negative feedback**. ✔

## 3. Open‑loop ("A") circuit (load $R_F$ on both ports, neglect feed‑forward and $r_o$)

- Input node: $R_{in,open} = R_F \| \tfrac{1}{g_{m1}}$ (CG input resistance), so $v_S = I_{in}(R_F\|\tfrac1{g_{m1}})$
- Middle: $v_X = g_{m1}R_{D1}v_S$
- Output: $v_{out} = -g_{m2}(R_{D2}\|R_F)v_X$, $R_{out,open} = R_{D2}\|R_F$

$$R_0 \equiv \frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}} = -\,g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}\,(R_{D2}\|R_F)\,\frac{R_F}{1+g_{m1}R_F}$$

## 4. Loop gain

The feedback network returns $i_{RF}\approx v_{out}/R_F$, so $K = 1/R_F$ and

$$T = -\frac{R_0}{R_F} = \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\|R_F)}{1+g_{m1}R_F}\qquad(\text{i.e. } R_0 = -T R_F)$$

## 5. Closed‑loop results (shunt–shunt ⇒ both impedances divided by $1+T$)

$$\boxed{\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{R_0}{1+T} = -R_F\,\frac{T}{1+T} \;\xrightarrow{T\gg1}\; -R_F}$$

$$R_{in} = \frac{R_F\|\tfrac{1}{g_{m1}}}{1+T}\;\;(\text{very small, ideal for a current input}),\qquad
R_{out} = \frac{R_{D2}\|R_F}{1+T}\;\;(\text{very small, ideal for a voltage output})$$

**Ideal limit intuition:** deep feedback forces $v_S \to 0$ (virtual ground at the input node); then essentially all of $I_{in}$ is steered through $R_F$ into the output node ($i_{RF} \approx -I_{in}$), giving $V_{out} \approx -I_{in}R_F$ — the gain is set by the passive resistor $R_F$ alone, hence accurate and stable. Bandwidth is likewise extended by $(1+T)$.

## 6. Exact node solution (verification)

With $G = g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$, KCL at nodes S, X, Out gives

$$\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{R_F R_{D2}(1-G R_F)}{(R_{D2}+R_F)(1+g_{m1}R_F) - R_{D2}(1-G R_F)} \approx \frac{-R_F}{1+\dfrac{(1+g_{m1}R_F)(R_{D2}+R_F)}{G\,R_{D2}R_F}}$$

which is exactly $R_0/(1+T)$ plus a negligible feed‑forward term $-1/(GR_F)$ — confirming the feedback analysis.

## 7. Bias remarks

$V_b$ fixes M₁'s gate; the DC path through $R_F$ also closes a DC feedback loop that stabilizes the operating points: $V_X = V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}$ biases M₂'s gate, and $V_{out,DC} = V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D2}$.

**Summary:** two‑stage CG+CS amplifier with shunt–shunt (voltage‑sampling, current‑mixing) negative feedback through $R_F$ → a transimpedance amplifier with gain $\approx -R_F$, and input/output resistances lowered by $(1+T)$, making it an ideal current‑input, voltage‑output interface (e.g., photodiode/readout front end).

## Circuit description (what each element does)

- **M₁** is a **common‑gate (CG) stage**: the input current I_in is injected into its source; its gate is held at the fixed bias V_b (an AC ground). Its drain load is R_D1, so node X sees v_X = +g_m1 R_D1·v_in (non‑inverting).
- **M₂** is a **common‑source (CS) stage**: it amplifies v_X and delivers v_out = −g_m2 v_X·(load) (inverting). R_D2 is its drain load.
- **R_F** connects the output node back to the input node (source of M₁): it is the **feedback network**.
- The signal chain CG → CS gives a net **inverting** voltage gain from the input node to the output node, so the current returned through R_F opposes disturbances at the input node → **negative feedback** (as confirmed below).

## Feedback topology

- At the **output**, R_F ties directly to the V_out node → it **samples the output voltage** (shunt/shunt sensing).
- At the **input**, R_F returns a **current** that sums with I_in at the low‑impedance input node (shunt/shunt mixing).

⇒ **Shunt–shunt (voltage–current) feedback**: the circuit is a **transimpedance amplifier (current‑in, voltage‑out)**. Consistently, feedback *lowers* both input and output impedances, which is exactly what a good I→V converter wants.

## Loop gain (load R_F at both ports, neglect feed‑forward through R_F; λ = γ = 0)

- Open‑loop input resistance: R_in,open = (1/g_m1) ∥ R_F, so v_in = i_in·R_in,open
- Forward path: v_X = g_m1 R_D1 v_in; v_out = −g_m2 v_X·(R_D2 ∥ R_F)

$$A = \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = -\frac{g_{m1}R_F}{1+g_{m1}R_F}\; g_{m2}R_{D1}\,(R_{D2}\parallel R_F)$$

- Feedback factor (returned current per output voltage): K = 1/R_F, hence

$$T = |A|K = \frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}\,(R_{D2}\parallel R_F)}{R_F + 1/g_{m1}}$$

## Closed‑loop results

- **Transimpedance gain:**

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = \frac{A}{1+T} \;\xrightarrow{\;T\gg1\;}\; -R_F$$

- **Input resistance:** R_in = [(1/g_m1) ∥ R_F]/(1+T) → very small (ideal current input).
- **Output resistance:** R_out = (R_D2 ∥ R_F)/(1+T) → very small (ideal voltage output).

(Exact node analysis, keeping feed‑forward through R_F, gives v_out/i_in = P(1−G·R_F)/[1+g_m1R_F+P·G−P/R_F], with P = R_D2∥R_F and G = g_m1 g_m2 R_D1, which reduces to the expressions above.)

## Physical intuition

Negative feedback forces the input node (source of M₁) to a **virtual ground**. Since v_in ≈ 0, M₁ carries almost no signal current, and essentially all of i_in is steered through R_F. The feedback loop then drives the output to v_out ≈ −i_in·R_F so that the R_F current exactly absorbs i_in — precisely the operation of a transimpedance (current‑to‑voltage) amplifier, with the two transistor stages supplying the loop gain that makes the virtual ground accurate.

**Summary:** two‑stage CG+CS amplifier with resistive shunt–shunt feedback ⇒ a transimpedance amplifier with gain ≈ −R_F, loop gain T = g_m2 R_D1(R_D2∥R_F)/(R_F+1/g_m1), and both input and output impedances reduced by (1+T).

The circuit shown is a two-stage MOSFET amplifier with feedback. Here is a detailed analysis:

**1. Component Identification and Topology:**
*   **Transistors:**
    *   **$M_1$:** The arrow on the source terminal points away from the gate (down-left), indicating an **NMOS** transistor. It is configured as a **Common Gate (CG)** amplifier. Its gate is biased by a DC voltage $V_b$. Its source is the input node, and its drain is connected to node $X$.
    *   **$M_2$:** The arrow on the source terminal points away from the gate (down), indicating an **NMOS** transistor. It is configured as a **Common Source (CS)** amplifier. Its gate is driven by node $X$ (the output of the first stage). Its source is grounded, and its drain is the output node $V_{out}$.
*   **Resistors:**
    *   **$R_{D1}$ and $R_{D2}$:** These are drain load resistors connected to the supply voltage $V_{DD}$.
    *   **$R_F$:** This is a feedback resistor connecting the output node $V_{out}$ to the input node (source of $M_1$).
*   **Sources:**
    *   **$I_{in}$:** A current source connected to the input node (source of $M_1$) and ground. The arrow points upwards, indicating it sources current into the circuit.
    *   **$V_{DD}$:** The positive supply voltage.
    *   **$V_b$:** A DC bias voltage for the gate of $M_1$.

**2. Circuit Operation:**
*   **Input Stage ($M_1$):** The input is a current $I_{in}$ injected into the source of $M_1$. Since the gate $V_b$ is fixed (AC ground), this is a Common Gate configuration. The transconductance $g_{m1}$ converts the source voltage change (caused by $I_{in}$) into a drain current change.
    *   If $I_{in}$ increases (flows up), the source voltage $V_s$ rises.
    *   For an NMOS, $V_{gs} = V_g - V_s = V_b - V_s$. If $V_s$ rises, $V_{gs}$ decreases.
    *   This reduces the drain current $I_{d1}$.
*   **Output Stage ($M_2$):** The drain of $M_1$ (node $X$) drives the gate of $M_2$.
    *   Node $X$ is connected to $V_{DD}$ via $R_{D1}$.
    *   If $I_{d1}$ decreases, the voltage drop across $R_{D1}$ decreases, so $V_X$ rises (assuming current flows $V_{DD} \to X$). Wait, for NMOS $M_1$, current flows Drain $\to$ Source (Down). So $I_{d1}$ leaves $X$. $R_{D1}$ current enters $X$. So $V_X = V_{DD} - I_{d1}R_{D1}$. If $I_{d1} \downarrow$, $V_X \uparrow$.
    *   $M_2$ is a Common Source amplifier. $V_{gs2} = V_X$.
    *   If $V_X$ rises, $M_2$ turns on harder ($I_{d2}$ increases).
    *   $V_{out} = V_{DD} - I_{d2}R_{D2}$.
    *   If $I_{d2}$ increases, $V_{out}$ decreases.
*   **Feedback:**
    *   The output voltage $V_{out}$ is fed back to the input node via $R_F$.
    *   The feedback current $i_{RF}$ flows from the input node to $V_{out}$ (indicated by the arrow).
    *   $i_{RF} = (V_s - V_{out}) / R_F$.
    *   If $V_{out}$ decreases (due to increased $I_{in}$), and $V_s$ increases, the difference $(V_s - V_{out})$ increases.
    *   So $i_{RF}$ increases (flows more strongly from input to output).
    *   At the input node, KCL: $I_{in} = I_{s1} + i_{RF}$. (Assuming $I_{in}$ flows in, $I_{s1}$ and $i_{RF}$ flow out).
    *   If $i_{RF}$ increases, $I_{s1}$ (drain current of $M_1$) must decrease to satisfy KCL (since $I_{in}$ is constant).
    *   $I_{s1}$ decreasing means $M_1$ turns off more.
    *   This implies $V_s$ must rise further (to reduce $V_{gs}$).
    *   This reinforces the initial change ($V_s \uparrow$).

**3. Conclusion on Feedback Polarity:**
*   The circuit exhibits **Positive Feedback** (Regenerative Feedback).
*   An increase in input current $I_{in}$ leads to a decrease in $V_{out}$, which in turn drives the input node voltage $V_s$ higher, further increasing the effect.
*   This suggests the circuit acts as a **Regenerative Comparator** or a **Latch**. It will have hysteresis. Once the input current exceeds a certain threshold, the output will swing rapidly to a low state (or high state, depending on bias). The positive feedback accelerates this transition.

**4. Alternative Interpretation (if $M_1$ is PMOS):**
*   If the arrow on $M_1$ points *in* (PMOS), the analysis changes slightly but likely leads to the same conclusion of positive feedback given the $I_{in}$ direction.
*   However, the arrow points *out*, so $M_1$ is NMOS.

**5. Summary:**
*   **Circuit Type:** Two-stage amplifier with positive feedback.
*   **Input:** Current $I_{in}$.
*   **Output:** Voltage $V_{out}$.
*   **Function:** Likely a **Current Comparator** or **Regenerative Transimpedance Amplifier**.
*   **Stages:**
    1.  $M_1$ (Common Gate) acts as the input transconductance stage.
    2.  $M_2$ (Common Source) acts as the voltage gain stage.
*   **Feedback:** Resistor $R_F$ provides positive feedback, creating a hysteresis loop (Schmitt Trigger behavior).

**Note on Bias:**
*   $V_b$ sets the operating point of $M_1$.
*   $R_{D1}$ and $R_{D2}$ set the DC drain voltages.
*   $I_{in}$ sets the DC bias current for the input node.

If the arrow on $I_{in}$ were pointing down (current sink), the feedback would be negative, making it a stable Transimpedance Amplifier. Given the arrow points up, it is a regenerative circuit.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as the common-source stage, and RF as connecting output to input. But it reverses the feedback polarity: this is negative feedback, not regenerative positive feedback, so the central circuit conclusion is wrong.

Based on the provided circuit diagram, here is an analysis of the circuit.

### 1. Circuit Overview and Topology
The circuit is a two-stage analog amplifier that functions as a **Transimpedance Amplifier (TIA)** or the input stage of a **Current Feedback Amplifier (CFA)**.
*   **Input:** A current source $I_{in}$.
*   **Output:** A voltage $V_{out}$.
*   **Feedback:** A resistor $R_F$ provides feedback from the output to the input node.

### 2. Component Identification
*   **$M_1$ (PMOS Transistor):**
    *   The symbol shows an arrow on the source terminal pointing *inwards* towards the gate, which is the standard symbol for a **PMOS** transistor.
    *   **Configuration:** It is configured as a **Common Gate (CG)** amplifier.
        *   **Gate:** Biased by a DC voltage $V_b$.
        *   **Source:** Connected to the input current source $I_{in}$ and the feedback resistor $R_F$. This is the low-impedance input node.
        *   **Drain:** Connected to node $X$.
*   **$M_2$ (NMOS Transistor):**
    *   The symbol shows an arrow on the source terminal pointing *outwards* (downwards), which is the standard symbol for an **NMOS** transistor.
    *   **Configuration:** It is configured as a **Common Source (CS)** amplifier.
        *   **Gate:** Connected to node $X$ (output of the first stage).
        *   **Source:** Connected to Ground.
        *   **Drain:** Connected to the output node $V_{out}$ and resistor $R_{D2}$.
*   **Resistors:**
    *   **$R_{D1}$:** Load resistor for $M_1$, connected between $V_{DD}$ and node $X$.
    *   **$R_{D2}$:** Load resistor for $M_2$, connected between $V_{DD}$ and the drain of $M_2$ ($V_{out}$).
    *   **$R_F$:** Feedback resistor connecting the input node (Source of $M_1$) to the output node ($V_{out}$).
*   **$I_{in}$:** An ideal current source pointing upwards, injecting current into the circuit.

### 3. Operation Analysis
*   **Input Stage ($M_1$):**
    *   The input current $I_{in}$ is injected into the source of $M_1$.
    *   Since $M_1$ is a Common Gate stage, its input impedance is low (approx. $1/g_{m1}$). This makes the source node a good summing junction for currents.
    *   The current $I_{in}$ flows through $M_1$ to the drain node $X$.
    *   The current then flows through $R_{D1}$ to $V_{DD}$.
    *   This converts the input current into a voltage change at node $X$ ($V_X$). Specifically, $V_X \approx V_{DD} - I_{D1} R_{D1}$. Since $I_{D1} \approx I_{in}$, $V_X$ is proportional to the input current (Transimpedance behavior).
*   **Output Stage ($M_2$):**
    *   The voltage $V_X$ is applied to the gate of $M_2$.
    *   $M_2$ acts as a voltage amplifier (Common Source).
    *   Changes in $V_X$ modulate the drain current $I_{D2}$, which in turn changes the voltage at $V_{out}$ across $R_{D2}$.
*   **Feedback:**
    *   The resistor $R_F$ connects the output voltage $V_{out}$ back to the input node.
    *   This is a **Shunt-Shunt Feedback** configuration (Voltage sampling, Current mixing).
    *   In a functional Current Feedback Amplifier, this feedback stabilizes the gain and lowers the input impedance. The gain is primarily determined by $R_F$.

### 4. DC Biasing
*   $V_{DD}$ provides the high voltage rail.
*   $V_b$ sets the gate-source voltage of $M_1$, controlling its operating current.
*   $I_{in}$ provides the signal current.
*   The circuit establishes DC operating points for $M_1$ and $M_2$ such that they are in the saturation (active) region.

### 5. Summary of Function
This circuit is designed to convert an input current $I_{in}$ into an output voltage $V_{out}$.
*   The **Common Gate** stage ($M_1$) provides a low input impedance, allowing the input current $I_{in}$ to be summed with the feedback current.
*   The **Common Source** stage ($M_2$) provides voltage gain.
*   The feedback resistor $R_F$ determines the overall transimpedance gain ($V_{out} / I_{in}$). In an ideal CFA/TIA with high open-loop gain, the gain is approximately $R_F$.

**Note on Feedback Polarity:**
Based on the standard symbols ($M_1$ PMOS, $M_2$ NMOS, resistors to $V_{DD}$), the open-loop gain appears to be positive, which would imply positive feedback. However, in standard CFA designs, the input stage is usually arranged to provide negative feedback. This might imply that $M_1$ is intended to be an NMOS transistor (arrow pointing out) or the current source $I_{in}$ is a sink, or the load resistors are connected to ground. Assuming standard functional design, it operates as a negative feedback amplifier. Given the symbols as drawn ($M_1$ PMOS, $M_2$ NMOS), the feedback loop analysis suggests positive feedback, which would make this an oscillator or latch circuit, unless there's a subtle interpretation of the biasing (e.g. $V_b$ being the signal input). However, the most standard interpretation is a **Current Feedback Amplifier input stage**.

However, it explicitly concludes that the circuit has positive feedback, contrary to the actual negative-feedback mechanism, so the golden solution caps the score at 2.
